items.source: example sentences on the A2-1B vocabulary cards; in no unit vocabulary list
items.notes: Not interchangeable with veya / ya da, which is why it is a separate entry rather than a duplicate: Turkish splits 'or' exactly as Finnish splits tai and vai. yoksa joins the alternatives inside a question — “Siyah zeytin mi yoksa yeşil zeytin mi?” — while veya / ya da joins them in a statement. Dropped once as a duplicate and restored: the shared English gloss hides a distinction Turkish makes.

items.source: A1-5C grammar lesson (-DAn beri); phrase from the A2-3C card sentence “Sabahtan beri ders çalışıyorum”
items.notes: A grammar construction stored as a use case rather than a bare gloss: an isolated 'beri' or '-DAn daha' teaches nothing, while a phrase shows the suffix doing its work. Follows the existing “hem ... hem de” entry. The -DAn beri construction had no representation at all. Two forms are stored so the suffix is seen on different stems.

items.source: A1-5C coursebook grammar section, which gives this as its own example of -DAn beri
items.notes: A grammar construction stored as a use case rather than a bare gloss: an isolated 'beri' or '-DAn daha' teaches nothing, while a phrase shows the suffix doing its work. Follows the existing “hem ... hem de” entry. Second use case for -DAn beri, from the coursebook itself.

items.turkish: Ya kahve ya da çay içelim.
items.english: Let's drink either coffee or tea.
items.source: A2-4C coursebook grammar section (correlatives)
items.notes: Stored as a sentence for the same reason as the ne ... ne de card, and with the same plain vocabulary so the two can be compared directly. Distinct from veya / ya da, which joins two alternatives once rather than marking both. A2-4C.

items.turkish: Ne kahve ne de çay istiyorum.
items.english: I want neither coffee nor tea.
items.source: A2-4C coursebook grammar section (correlatives)
items.notes: Stored as a sentence, not the bare pattern “ne ... ne de”: the difficulty is that Turkish keeps the verb affirmative where English negates it, and a pattern card cannot show that. Vocabulary kept deliberately plain — kahve, çay, istemek are all long-known — so the attention falls on the grammar. A2-4C.
